title: Escape to Host
summary: Escape to host describes breaking out of a container or virtual machine to reach the system underneath. Isolation is enforced by kernel namespaces, control groups, hypervisor boundaries, and mandatory access control profiles, and an escape normally abuses a configuration mistake or a flaw in that boundary rather than the application inside it. Documented routes include starting a container that bind mounts the host filesystem, which lets the attacker write payloads and reach control utilities on the host, running a privileged container that can load a kernel module or alter kernel parameters, and abusing system calls for privilege escalation and secret theft. A mounted container management socket is another common path, because it hands the container the same control interface as the host. Detection is difficult after the fact and depends on runtime signals such as container processes spawning host binaries, unexpected writes to host paths, and kernel module loads.

beginner.definition: A container or a virtual machine is meant to keep its work separate from the machine it runs on. Escape to host means breaking that separation. The attacker gets out of the box and onto the real computer underneath it. From there they can reach everything else on that machine.
beginner.whyItMatters: The host usually holds many containers and much more sensitive data than any single one of them. If an attacker escapes, one small foothold becomes control of a whole server. Isolation settings are often loosened for convenience and never tightened again. Checking those settings now is far cheaper than cleaning up afterwards.
howItWorks: The attacker gains control of a container or a virtual machine first.
They examine what the container can reach, such as shared folders and devices.
If the host filesystem is mounted, they write files and schedule jobs on the host.
A privileged container may let them load a kernel module or change kernel settings.
A mounted management socket lets them ask the host to start another container for them.
Sometimes they instead take advantage of a flaw in the isolation software itself.
beginner.example: Picture a self storage building where each unit is locked and billed separately. One unit was built with a wall that is too thin, and nobody ever inspected it. A tenant notices, removes a panel, and steps into the corridor that runs behind all the units. From that corridor they can open any unit in the building. Nothing on their own door looked wrong, and their rent was paid. The problem was the wall, not the lock.
takeaways: Isolation depends on configuration, and a weak setting is enough to break it.
A privileged container or a mounted management socket is a serious risk.
Host level monitoring is what catches an escape, because the container looks normal.

objectives: Explain what isolation a container or virtual machine normally provides.
Describe how a host filesystem bind mount leads to host level access.
Explain the risk created by privileged containers and mounted management sockets.
Identify runtime telemetry that can indicate an escape attempt.
Summarise why host level visibility is essential for detection.
